'''Peter Michael Maitlis''', [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Crabtree |first=Robert H. |date=2023 |title=Peter M. Maitlis. 15 January 1933—18 May 2022 |journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society |volume=75|pages=327–343 |doi=10.1098/rsbm.2022.0048 |s2cid=258189933 |doi-access=free }}</ref> (15 January 1933 – 18 May 2022) was a British [[organometallic chemistry|organometallic]] [[chemist]].<ref name="shefhome">{{cite web|url=http://www.sheffield.ac.uk/chemistry/staff/profiles/maitlis.html|title=Emeritus Prof Peter Maitlis FRS|publisher=Department of Chemistry, [[University of Sheffield]]|accessdate=2011-02-03}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Maitlis was born on 15 January 1933,<ref name="pot">{{cite web|url=http://www.debretts.com/people/biographies/search/results/5390/Peter%20Michael+MAITLIS.aspx|title= Prof Peter Maitlis, FRS Authorised Biography|work=[[Debrett's People of Today]] |accessdate=2011-02-03}}</ref> in Berlin and educated at [[Hendon School]] (then Hendon County School) in north London 1944–50. He was awarded a [[Bachelor's degree]] in Science from the [[University of Birmingham]], and a PhD (1956, studying under Professor [[Michael J. S. Dewar]],<ref name = "metallomesogens">{{cite journal|title = Metallomesogens&nbsp;– Metal-Complexes in Organized Fluid Phases|author1 = Giroud-Godquin, A.-M.|author2 = Maitlis, P. M.|authorlink2 = Peter Maitlis|journal = [[Angewandte Chemie|Angew. Chem. Int. Ed.]]|volume = 30|issue = 4|pages = 375–402|year = 1991|doi = 10.1002/anie.199103751}}</ref> who helped to develop the [[Dewar–Chatt–Duncanson model]] for bonding in [[organometallic compound]]s) and a [[DSc]] (1970) from the [[University of London]].<ref name="shefhome" />

==Career==
After completing his doctorate, Maitlis worked as an [[assistant lecturer]] at the University of London.<ref name = "shefhome" /> He undertook [[postdoctoral]] study at [[Cornell University]] as a [[Fulbright fellow]] (1960–1961) and then as a [[research fellow]] at [[Harvard University]] (1961–1962)<ref name="pot" /> under [[F. Gordon A. Stone|F. G. A. Stone]].<ref>{{cite book|title = Leaving No Stone Unturned: Pathways in Organometallic Chemistry|author = Stone, F. G. A.|authorlink = F. Gordon A. Stone|year = 1993|publisher = [[American Chemical Society]]|location = Washington, D.C.|isbn = 978-0-8412-1826-0|page = 199}}</ref>

While working and teaching at [[McMaster University]] in [[Hamilton, Ontario]] (1962–1972), he rose from assistant professor to a full professorship. Returning to the United Kingdom in 1972, Maitlis was a professor of chemistry at the [[University of Sheffield]] for 30 years until his appointment as an [[emeritus professor]] in 2002.<ref name="pot"/>

In 1971, he published two volumes on the organic chemistry of [[palladium]]<ref>{{cite book|title = The Organic Chemistry of Palladium, Volume 1|author = Maitlis, P. M.|authorlink = Peter Maitlis|year = 1971|publisher = Academic Press|location = New York|isbn = 978-0-12-465802-8}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title = The Organic Chemistry of Palladium, Volume 2: Catalytic Reactions|author = Maitlis, P. M.|authorlink = Peter Maitlis|year = 1971|publisher = Academic Press|location = New York|isbn = 978-0-12-465802-8}}</ref> which were "widely recognised as the most authoritative account of the organo-complexes of this metal".<ref name = "citation" />

Maitlis was elected a [[fellow of the Royal Society]] in 1984.<ref>{{cite web|url = http://royalsociety.org/WorkArea/DownloadAsset.aspx?id=4294972811|title = List of Fellows of the Royal Society, 1660&nbsp;– 2007|website = royalsociety.org|publisher = [[Royal Society]]|accessdate=2011-02-04|page = 233|quote = Date of Election: 15/03/1984}}</ref> The citation highlights his work on the [[platinum group]] metals [[palladium]], [[rhodium]] and [[iridium]].<ref name = "citation">{{cite web|url = http://www2.royalsociety.org/DServe/dserve.exe?dsqIni=Dserve.ini&dsqApp=Archive&dsqDb=Catalog&dsqCmd=show.tcl&dsqSearch=%28RefNo==%22EC%2F1984%2F22%22%29|title = Certificates of Election and Candidature: Maitlis, Peter Michael|website = royalsociety.org|publisher = [[Royal Society]]|accessdate=2011-02-03|year = 1978}}</ref>

===Achievements in organometallic chemistry===
The [[hexafluorophosphate]] ion is generally considered inert and hence a suitable [[counterion]] in [[organometallic chemistry|organometallic synthesis]]. However, Maitlis' work has demonstrated a [[solvolysis]] reaction of the hexafluorophosphate ion. The tris([[solvent]]) [[organorhodium chemistry|rhodium]] complex [(η<sup>5</sup>-C<sub>5</sub>[[methyl|Me]]<sub>5</sub>)Rh(Me<sub>2</sub>CO)<sub>3</sub>](PF<sub>6</sub>)<sub>2</sub> undergoes solvolysis when heated in [[acetone]], forming a difluorophosphate-bridged complex [(η<sup>5</sup>-C<sub>5</sub>Me<sub>5</sub>)Rh(μ-OPF<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>3</sub>Rh(η<sup>5</sup>-C<sub>5</sub>Me<sub>5</sub>)]PF<sub>6</sub>.<ref>{{cite journal|author1 = Thompson, S. J.|author2 = Bailey, P. M.|author3 = White, C.|author4 = Maitlis, P. M.|authorlink4 = Peter Maitlis|year = 1976|title = Solvolysis of the Hexafluorophosphate Ion and the Structure of [Tris(μ-difluorophosphato)bis(penta-methylcyclopentadienylrhodium)] Hexafluorophosphate|journal = [[Angewandte Chemie|Angew. Chem. Int. Ed.]]|volume = 15|issue = 8|pages = 490–491|doi = 10.1002/anie.197604901}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author2= Thompson, S. J.|author1 = White, C.|author3 = Maitlis, P. M.|authorlink3 = Peter Maitlis|year = 1977|title = Pentamethylcyclopentadienyl-rhodium and -iridium Complexes '''''XIV.''''' The Solvolysis of Coordinated Acetone Solvent Species to Tris(μ-difluorophosphato)bis[η<sup>5</sup>-pentamethylcyclopentadienylrhodium(III)] Hexafluorophosphate, to the η<sup>5</sup>-(2,4-dimethyl-1-oxapenta-1,3-dienyl)(pentamethylcyclopentadienyl)iridium Cation, or to the η<sup>5</sup>-(2-hydroxy-4-methylpentadienyl)(η<sup>5</sup>-pentamethylcyclopentadienyl)iridium Cation|journal = [[J. Organomet. Chem.]]|volume = 134|issue = 3|pages = 319–325|doi = 10.1016/S0022-328X(00)93278-9}}</ref>

:[[File:Partial solvolysis of hexafluorophospate.PNG|Heating [(η<sup>5</sup>-C<sub>5</sub>Me<sub>5</sub>)Rh(Me<sub>2</sub>CO)<sub>3</sub>](PF<sub>6</sub>)<sub>2</sub> in acetone results in the formation of the complex [(η<sup>5</sup>-C<sub>5</sub>Me<sub>5</sub>)Rh(μ-OPF<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>3</sub>Rh(η<sup>5</sup>-C<sub>5</sub>Me<sub>5</sub>)]PF<sub>6</sub>]]

[[Dewar benzene#Hexamethyl Dewar benzene|Hexamethyl Dewar benzene]] (C<sub>6</sub>Me<sub>6</sub>) undergoes an unusual rearrangement reaction with [[hydrohalic acid]]s to form a [[pentamethylcyclopentadiene]] derivative,<ref>{{cite journal|author1 = Paquette, L. A.|author2 = Krow, G. R.|year = 1968|title = Electrophilic Additions to Hexamethyldewarbenzene|journal = [[Tetrahedron Letters|Tetrahedron Lett.]]|volume = 9|issue = 17|pages = 2139–2142|doi = 10.1016/S0040-4039(00)89761-0}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author1 = Criegee, R.|author2 = Gruner, H.|year = 1968|title = Acid-catalyzed Rearrangements of Hexamethyl-prismane and Hexamethyl-Dewar-benzene|journal = [[Angewandte Chemie|Angew. Chem. Int. Ed.]]|volume = 7|issue = 6|pages = 467–468|doi = 10.1002/anie.196804672}}</ref> and consequently can be used as a starting material for synthesising some [[Pentamethylcyclopentadiene#References|pentamethylcyclopentadienyl]] [[organometallic compound]]s.<ref>{{cite journal|author1 = Kang, J. W.|author2= Moseley, K.|author3 = Maitlis, P. M.|authorlink3 = Peter Maitlis|year = 1968|title = Mechanisms of Reactions of Dewar Hexamethylbenzene with Rhodium and Iridium Chlorides|journal = [[Chemical Communications|Chem. Commun.]]|issue = 21|pages = 1304–1305|doi = 10.1039/C19680001304}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author1 = Kang, J. W.|author2 = Maitlis, P. M.|authorlink2 = Peter Maitlis|year = 1968|title = Conversion of Dewar Hexamethylbenzene to Pentamethylcyclopentadienylrhodium(III) Chloride|journal = [[J. Am. Chem. Soc.]]|volume = 90|issue = 12|pages = 3259–3261|doi = 10.1021/ja01014a063| bibcode=1968JAChS..90.3259K }}</ref>

[[Image:Hexamethyl Dewar benzene reacting with rhodium chloride under acidic conditions.PNG|800px|frameless|center|Synthesis of the rhodium(III) dimer [Cp*RhCl<sub>2</sub>]<sub>2</sub> from hexamethyl Dewar benzene]]

Maitlis and colleagues demonstrated this synthesis and its applicability to the iridium [[analogue (chemistry)|analogue]], [[Pentamethylcyclopentadienyl iridium dichloride dimer|[(η<sup>5</sup>-C<sub>5</sub>Me<sub>5</sub>)IrCl<sub>2</sub>]<sub>2</sub>]].<ref>{{cite journal|title = Pentamethylcyclopentadienylrhodium and -iridium Halides. '''''I.''''' Synthesis and Properties|year = 1969|author1 = Kang, J. W.|author2 = Moseley, K.|author3 = Maitlis, P. M.|authorlink3 = Peter Maitlis|journal = [[J. Am. Chem. Soc.]]|volume = 91|issue = 22|pages = 5970–5977|doi = 10.1021/ja01050a008| bibcode=1969JAChS..91.5970K }}</ref> His group also demonstrated a more convenient synthesis for the bright orange, air-stable [[diamagnetic]] iridium reagent using [[pentamethylcyclopentadiene]].<ref>{{cite book|author1 = White, C.|author2 = Yates, A.|author3 = Maitlis, P. M.|authorlink3 = Peter Maitlis|author4 = Heinekey, D. M.| chapter=(η <sup>5</sup> -Pentamethylcyclopentadienyl)Rhodium and -Iridium Compounds | title=Inorganic Syntheses |series = [[Inorg. Synth.]]|volume = 29|pages = 228–234|doi = 10.1002/9780470132609.ch53| date=2007 |isbn = 9780470132609}}</ref>

[[Isocyanide]]s can serve as [[ligands]] in [[co-ordination chemistry]] as a result of the lone electron pair on [[carbon]], and are especially useful with metals in the 0, +1, and +2 [[oxidation state]]s. In particular, Maitlis has demonstrated that [[tert-butyl isocyanide|''tert''-butyl isocyanide]] can stabilise metals in unusual oxidation states, such as palladium(I) in the complex [(''t''-BuNC)<sub>2</sub>Pd(μ-Cl)]<sub>2</sub>.<ref>{{cite book|author1 = Rettig, M. F.|author2 = Maitlis, P. M.|authorlink2 = Peter Maitlis|authorlink3 = F. A. Cotton|author3 = Cotton, F. A.|author4 = Webb, T. R.| chapter=Tetrakis( ''tert'' -Butyl Isocyanide)Di-μ-Chlorodipalladium(I) | title=Inorganic Syntheses |series = [[Inorg. Synth.]]|volume = 28|pages = 110–113|doi = 10.1002/9780470132593.ch29| date=2007 |isbn = 9780470132593}}</ref>

===Metallomesogens===
[[Metallomesogen|Metallomesogens]] are "metal complexes of organic ligands which exhibit [[liquid crystal]]line ([[Mesophase|mesomorphic]]) character [and thus they] combine the variety and range of metal-based coordination chemistry with the extraordinary physical properties exhibited by liquid crystals."<ref name = "metallomesogens" /> They have been a research interest of Maitlis' group since the mid-1980s, and in fact Maitlis jointly directed the early investigations of these systems in the UK and actually coined the term ''metallomesogen''.<ref>{{cite journal|title = Synthesis and Characterisation of Rod-Like Metallomesogens of Mn(I) based on Schiff Base Ligands|author1 = Liu, X.-H.|author2 = Abser, M. N.|author3 = Bruce, D. W.|journal = [[J. Organomet. Chem.]]|volume = 551|issue = 1–2|year = 1998|pages = 271–280|doi = 10.1016/S0022-328X(97)00437-3|quote = Serious UK effort in this area started in 1984 in Sheffield and DWB remembers several early conversations with Peter Maitlis on the subject. ... perhaps the most interesting and satisfying results, at least from a pure liquid crystal perspective, were obtained with their complexes to silver—another of Peter's initial suggestions. The subject of this paper relates to organometallic ''metallomesogens''—a term coined by Peter—and is dedicated to him with much warmth and affection." (p.&nbsp;271)}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Maitlis was Jewish. He was the father of the journalist and newsreader [[Emily Maitlis]], and the psychologist and academic [[Sally Maitlis]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.thejc.com/news/features/emily-maitlis-getting-it-right-sfxk0l26|title=Emily Maitlis: Getting it right|work=[[The Jewish Chronicle]]|author= Ebner, Sarah|date = 19 April 2017|access-date = 21 November 2019}}</ref>

He died on 18 May 2022, at the age of 89.<ref>{{cite news |title=Maitlis, Peter |url=https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/births-marriages-and-deaths-may-31-2022-hdbn6wtcd |access-date=31 May 2022 |work=The Times |date=31 May 2022}}</ref>
